sec.title: Background
sec.p: Glycoprotein A-repetitions predominant (GARP) is a cell surface non-signaling receptor for docking and activating latent transforming growth factor beta (LTGFβ) expressed by regulatory T cells, platelets, and tumor cells. In lung and breast cancers, its expression correlates with advanced stage and poor prognosis—suggesting that GARP could act as a therapeutic target. This study examines the therapeutic impact of targeting GARP in glioblastoma (GBM) via a novel anti-GARP chimeric antigen receptor-expressing T cell (CAR-T) modality in murine models of GBM.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We examined multiple human glioma databases to correlate the expression of GARP with clinical outcomes. We then performed multi-plex imaging of human GBM samples to understand the impact of GARP expression on the tumor microenvironment (TME). Importantly, we developed a novel anti-GARP CAR-T cell strategy to treat GBM. We examine if this therapy is efficacious against orthotopic models of GBM, in both immunocompetent syngeneic and immunodeficient mice.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We demonstrate that elevated GARP expression in human GBM correlates with poor overall survival, mesenchymal subtype, and gene signatures associated with angiogenesis and immune exclusion in the TME. Our novel anti-GARP CAR-T is efficacious in vitro and in vivo, against multiple preclinical models of GBM, including patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models without significant toxicity.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: GARP-LTGFβ plays a key role in the development and prognostics of GBM, and GARP-targeted CAR-T therapy shows promising efficacy and safety in murine orthotopic GBM models. A first-in-human phase I clinical trial for patients with recurrent GBM began to enroll patients in May 2025 (NCT06964737).
Keywords: GARP, TGFβ, CAR-T cells, glioblastoma, cancer immunotherapy

list-item.p: GARP is a novel and promising target for CAR-T therapy in glioblastoma.
GARP expression predicts poor outcomes and is highly enriched in glioma stem cells.

boxed-text.p: Glioblastoma remains a difficult-to-treat tumor type that exhibits poor responsiveness to immunotherapy; therein, further insights into the biology and development of new immunotherapy modalities for GBM are warranted. This study highlights the clinical relevance and therapeutic targetability of GARP-TGFβ axis in GBM while documenting preclinical efficacy and safety for GARP-targeted CAR-T immunotherapy. Collectively, our findings support further development of anti-GARP CAR-T cells for the treatment of GBM and address clinically unmet needs in brain cancer.

body.p: Glioma is the most common malignant primary tumor of the central nervous system, afflicting 3.19 per 100,000 people per year in the United States.1–3 The prognosis for high-grade glioma (HGG) remains dismal at less than 2 years survival following diagnosis. Low-grade glioma (LGG) represents an earlier disease stage, which will inevitably progress.3,4 The most well-studied and common forms of HGG are grade IV astrocytoma or glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), which present a significant therapeutic challenge due to their molecular heterogeneity, low neoantigen burden, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), and therapeutic resistance.5–10

Based on expression or mutation of EGFR, NF1, PDGFRA, or IDH1, GBM can be classified into classical, mesenchymal, proneural, and neural subtypes.7,11 The mesenchymal subtype exhibits enrichment in infiltrating immune cell populations, including regulatory T cells and tumor-associated macrophages, relative to proneural or classical subtypes.12 Proneural gliomas, particularly IDH1-mutant astrocytomas, harbor the highest frequency of IDH1 mutations and may respond to IDH1 inhibitors. TP53 mutations are common in the proneural subtype and can also be found in mesenchymal gliomas.7 The mesenchymal subtype of GBM exhibits the poorest overall survival while the proneural subtype correlates to better survival but younger patient age.6,13 The current standard of care for patients with newly diagnosed GBM includes maximal tumor resection, radiotherapy with concomitant temozolomide (TMZ) chemotherapy (Stupp protocol)14,15 and maintenance treatment with TMZ and tumor treating fields (TTF).16 Despite ongoing research, the overall survival (OS) for patients diagnosed with GBM has not improved significantly in two decades, especially for patients with relapsed diseases. Therein, new treatments and alternative strategies are urgently needed.

Genetic engineering of T cell receptors (TCRs) led to the development of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy (CAR-T),17,18 comprised of antigen-specific single-chain variable fragments (scFvs) of antibodies fused to T cell signaling domains transduced into T cells.19–21 CAR-T can bind tumor-specific antigens without major histocompatibility complex (MHC) restriction, allowing fully primed CAR-T to infiltrate tumors and perform antitumor effector functions. To date, most clinical success with CAR-T therapy has been reported in hematologic cancers22,23; however, ongoing research aims to identify new antigens to target a range of solid malignancies, including GBM.24

CAR-T-targeted antigens in GBM include interleukin-13 receptor alpha2 (IL13Rα2),25 epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (EGFRvIII),26 human epidermal growth factor 2 (HER2),27 erythropoietin-producing hepatocellular carcinoma A2 (EphA2)28, and others. Recently, a new T cell modality expressing a CAR to target EGFRvIII and secreting T-cell–engaging antibodies for wild-type EGFR, showed profound but transient responses in a phase 1 trial.29 No CAR-T products have shown conclusive, robust benefit in larger GBM trials.29–33 Therein, further study into CAR-T-targetable tumor antigens in GBM is needed.

Transforming growth factor β (TGFβ) is an essential cytokine that is highly expressed in tumors and facilitates immune evasion through multiple mechanisms.34–36 TGFβ stimulates cancer-associated fibroblast collagen production, trapping T cells in the periphery, restricting their cytotoxic function.37 Moreover, TGFβ induces differentiation of immunosuppressive regulatory T cells (Tregs), M2 macrophages, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells that stunt antitumor immunity.35,38–41 TGFβ also directly inhibits CD8+ T cells by blunting cytotoxic gene programs, limiting trafficking, and attenuating TCR stimulation.39,42 Thus, TGFβ offers an attractive target for immunotherapy. However, long-term inhibition of TGFβ induces inflammatory, autoimmune, and cardiovascular side effects43 with systemic inhibition via TGFβ-trap or small molecule inhibitors proven clinically unsuccessful.44–46 Thus, uncovering innovative approaches for targeting tumor-localized TGFβ is of strategic importance.

Glycoprotein-A repetitions predominant (GARP), encoded by LRRC32, is a cell surface, non-signaling, docking and activating receptor for latent TGFβ (LTGFβ).47,48 Expressed by platelets, activated Tregs, mesenchymal stromal, and tumor cells,42 GARP is an important post-translational regulator of TGFβ biogenesis. GARP associates with latency-associated peptide (LAP) of LTGFβ in cooperation with integrins to activate LTGFβ.35,49,50 We previously demonstrated that GARP is highly expressed by various primary human solid tumors but not normal epithelial cells.42,47,51,52 Using immunohistochemistry, Zimmer et al reported elevated GARP expression in GBM but not normal brain.53 Furthermore, we demonstrated that genetic deletion of Lrrc32 in murine Tregs or platelets—both of which infiltrate the TME—enhanced tumor control in colitis-associated and MC38 colon cancers.52,54,55 These findings suggest GARP expression in the TME may elevate the local concentration of active TGFβ and promote immune evasion.56,57 This work led to our development of a humanized anti-GARP monoclonal antibody (PIIO-1) that binds to the LAP binding pocket of GARP, ablating the GARP-TGFβ signaling axis by preventing LTGFβ-GARP association.56,58 Due to GARP’s selective expression in GBM, we hypothesized that the single-chain variable fragment (scFv) of PIIO-1 can target recurrent GBM by incorporating it into a CAR-T platform. Herein, we examine the role GARP plays in LGG and HGG and report a novel, safe anti-GARP CAR-T therapy with preclinical efficacy against GBM.

sec.title: Public GBM data collection and analysis
sec.p: Gene expression matrix values, survival, and clinicopathological information from the TCGA, CCGA, and IVY-GAP cohorts were obtained from TCGA, Broad Firehose GDAC, and GlioVis repositories. For survival analysis, LRRC32-high group was defined as samples with above median, and LRRC32-low group was defined as samples with below median relative transcript expression unless otherwise specified.

For the TCGA-GBM-2013 dataset, LRRC32-high group was defined by the top 10%, and LRRC32-low group was defined by the bottom ten percent of LRRC32 expression. GSVA enrichment scoring was performed via the GSVA package (v.1.49). For gene set enrichment analysis, differentially expressed genes enriched in patients with elevated LRRC32 expression were analyzed via the WEB-based Gene set analysis toolkit (WEBGESTALT) with weight set cover redundancy removal and multiple testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg procedure).

Spatial expression correlation analysis of LRRC32 was performed via the IVY-GAP GBM dataset. For protein abundance ratio analysis, patients were stratified by LRRC32 expression from the Glioblastoma CPTAC 2021 cohort and expression of protein abundance analyzed. Immune deconvolution was performed via the tumor immune estimation resource interface with RSEM-normalized mRNA expression values and clinical annotations sourced from the Broad Firehose GDAC database. For differential expression analysis of LRRC32 across normal human tissues, LRRC32 mRNA expression values were sourced from the human genotype-tissue expression (GTEX) database. Expression correlation analysis between LRRC32 and stem cell-associated genes was performed via the GlioVis interface from the CCGA GBM cohort.

sec.title: GSC ATAC-seq data collection and visualization
sec.p: The human GSC ATAC-seq datasets aligned on hg19 reference genome with bigwig format were downloaded from GSE163853. Twelve oncological treatment naïve samples were selected, including U3005MG-1, U3005MG-2, U3008MG-1, U3008MG-2, U3046MG-1, U3046MG-2, U3056MG-1, U3056MG-2, U3164MG-1, U3164MG-2, U3085MG-1, and U3085MG-2. GSE163853.

sec.title: Cell lines
sec.p: Human GBM U87-MG and DK-MG cell lines were obtained from ATCC; Mouse glioma GL261 was obtained from NCI Tumor Repository (Frederik, MD), and CT-2A from EMD Millipore. Cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). Patient-derived GBM xenografts hGBM-PDX #46 and hGBM-PDX #242 were obtained from the Mayo Clinic brain tumor patient-derived xenograft national resource.

sec.title: Construction of retroviral and lentiviral vectors
sec.p: The antibody targeting human GARP (PIIO-1) was reported previously.38 Synthetic oligonucleotide encoding for the GGGGSGGGGSGGGGS linker sequence joined to the PIIO-1 scFv VH and VL sequences was fused to the CD8a hinge and transmembrane domains, and 4-1BB and CD3ζ intracellular signaling domains. This scFv CAR construct was synthesized by GeneScript and cloned into BglII/SalI Sites of the MSCV-IRES-Thy1.1 DEST vector (Addgene, plasmid #17442) or XmaI/PacI sites of a modified pLenti-EF1alpha vector to generate the anti-GARP CAR lentiviral vector (pLenti-PIIO-1-CAR). For GARP overexpression, human LRRC32 cDNA was amplified and subcloned into EGFP-flanking NheI/BstBI sites of Addgenes’s pLJM1-EGFP (Plasmid #19319).

sec.title: Lentiviral and retroviral generation of human and mouse GARP CAR-T cells
sec.p: For lentiviruses, HEK293FT cells were transfected with Addgene’s pCMV-VSV-G (Plasmid #8454), pCMV-dR8.9 (Plasmid #8455), and pLenti-EF1alpha-scFv (PIIO-1)-CAR using TransIT-293 Reagent or Lipofectamine 3000. For retrovirus, Plat-E cells were transfected with MSCV-Thy1.1 PIIO-1 CAR using lipofectamine 3000. Viral supernatant was filtered (0.45 μm) and concentrated via amicon ultrafiltration (100 kDa) followed by T cell spin-transduction (800g x 90 minutes). Human T cells were enriched via a Pan T Cell Isolation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, Auburn, CA) from healthy donor PBMC and mouse T cells isolated from C57BL/6 spleens via a T Cell-specific Isolation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat# 130-095-130) prior to stimulation with anti-CD3/CD28 beads (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA) and IL-2 (Peprotech, Rocky Hill, NJ, 100 IU/ml), and lentiviral transduction (24 hr in TexMAX medium).

sec.title: Flow cytometric analysis
sec.p: For human CAR expression, 1 × 106 CAR-T or control T cells transduced with empty were stained with Protein L-PE conjugate (AcroBioSystems, Newark, DE) at 4 °C for 30 minutes, along with fluorochrome-labeled antibodies against CD4 and CD8 (eBiosciences). To detect CAR expression in murine T-cells, 1 × 106 CAR-T cells or control T cells were stained with anti-Thy1.1 antibody. To detect human GARP surface expression on GBM cell lines, cells were stained with anti-GARP antibody conjugated with phycoerythrin (PE, Biolegend).

sec.title: In vitro cytotoxicity assay
sec.p: The ability of GARP-specific CAR-T to kill luciferase-expressing targets cells was tested in a 24-h luciferase-based killing assay in 96-well flat-bottom plates at various effector: target ratio. Target cells alone were seeded to determine maximal luciferase expression (relative light units; RLUmax). After 24 h, 100 μl of supernatant was replaced with 100 μl of luciferase substrate (Bright-Glo, Promega) and RLU was measured after five minutes using the Spectra Max ID5 plate reader (Molecular Devices, San Jose, CA). Lysis was determined as [1—(RLUsample)/(RLUmax)] × 100. Killing of luciferase negative cells was measured with a 24-h lactase dehydrogenase (LDH)-based killing assay (Invitrogen Cat# C20301) in 96-well flat bottom plates at various effector-to-target ratios, per manufacturer’s instructions. Lysis was determined as [(LDH sample-Target Only sample)/(Max LDH sample-Target Only sample)] × 100.

sec.title: Cytokine ELISA
sec.p: Cytokine release assays were performed by coculturing 5 × 104 CAR-T or Control T cells with 5 × 104 target cells in triplicate in 96-well flat-bottom plates in a final volume of 200 μl of T cell media without cytokines. After 16–18 h, coculture supernatants were assayed via commercially available ELISA Kits, according to the manufacturer’s instructions (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN).

sec.title: Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF)
sec.p: Deidentified paraffin-embedded slides from patients with known glioblastoma or matched LGG and HGG specimens were obtained from the Ohio State University Department of Pathology under an IRB-approved protocol (OSU IRB# 2020C0062). Commercially available tissue microarrays supplemented primary samples (USBiomax, Inc. [Cat# GL1002, GL803d, BS17016b]). Multiplex immunofluorescence was performed using Vectra Polaris Automated Quantitative Pathology Imaging System (Akoya Biosciences) according to manufacturer protocols.

sec.title: Multiplex immunofluorescence image analysis
sec.p: qtiff mIF images were uploaded into InForm Tissue Analysis software (Akoya Biosciences) with representative sections from each sample used as a training set for image processing algorithm development. Regions of tissues were segmented into “high-GARP” (> 250 GARP-positive cells/mm2) and “low-GARP” (< 250 GARP-positive cells/mm2) via algorithm training until the accuracy calculated by the program was > 97%. After tissue segmentation, cell segmentation, and phenotyping were performed via a machine learning pipeline. After full quantification of each sample image, the data were analyzed using the R4.3.0 plugin phenoptr Reports (Akoya Biosciences).

sec.title: In vivo studies
sec.p: All animal experiments were carried out under the National Institutes of Health guide for the care and use of Laboratory animals and conducted with the approval of the Ohio State University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. Immunocompromised NOD-scid IL2Rgnull (NSG) mice were obtained from Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME, USA). Immunocompetent hLRRC32KI C57BL/6 mice were reported previously.56 Murine GBMs were established by intracranial injections of 5 × 104 luciferase-expressing cells for U87-WT, U87-hGARP, GL261-WT, GL261-hGARP, CT2A-WT, or CT2A-hGARP or 3 × 105 cells for DK-MG. Bioluminescent imaging was performed via Xenogen IVIS Spectrum (Caliper Life Sciences, Waltham, MA) 1 week after injection to confirm tumor engraftment; after confirmation of intracranial tumor burden, mice were randomized to treatment groups based on average tumor luminescence intensity, and treatments with CAR-T or control T cells were performed by intra-tumoral injection. CAR-T doses were adjusted based on CAR+ percentage determined via flow cytometry using Protein L-PE (AcroBioSystems). Mice were observed daily and sacrificed when neurological symptoms developed, body score decreased, or at defined time points for histology or other analyses. For survival analysis, mice were observed for up to 100 days or until endpoint criteria.

For bioluminescent imaging, animals received intraperitoneal injection of 100 μL 15 mg/mL D-Luciferin, Potassium Salt (Gold Biotechnology, St. Louis, MO, USA; Cat. No. Luck-100) under isoflurane gas. Images were obtained 5-10 minutes after luciferin administration. Bioluminescence intensity was quantified using Living Image Software (version 3.1, Caliper, Waltham, MA). Signal intensity was quantified as the sum of detected photons per second within the region of interest.

sec.title: Retrogenix screening of anti-GARP
sec.p: Retrogenix screening of the GARP-targeting PIIO-1 antibody was performed at 20 µg/ml by Charles River Laboratories. Briefly, the PIIO-1 antibody was screened for binding, against fixed HEK293 cells expressing 6111 individual human plasma membrane proteins, secreted and cell surface tethered human secreted proteins, and 403 human heterodimers arrayed across cell microarray slide sets. Detection was performed with an AlexaFluor647 anti-hIgG Fc. Twelve library interactions were identified with a median signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) (normalized against secondary-only control).

For confirmation screening, vectors encoding all interactors identified in the library screen, plus control vectors encoding CD20 and EGFR, were spotted on new slides. HEK293 cells were then reverse-transfected and treated with 20 µg/mL of PII0-1-hIgG4-S228P, 1 µg/mL of Rituximab biosimilar (positive control), or no test molecule (secondary only; negative control). Interactions were categorized as specific or non-specific (ie, interaction also observed with the negative control). Specific significant interactions were defined as interaction with median SNR ≥ 1.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed with GraphPad PRISM via independent sample t testing, paired sample t testing, Wilcoxon Rank-sum testing, and mixed effect model/ANOVA. Survival curves were plotted using the Kaplan–Meier method, and log-rank tests were used to compare curves between groups. P values are represented as *P < .05; **P < .01, ***P < .001 and ****P < .0001.

sec.title: Elevated GARP expression in human glioblastoma correlates with reduced overall survival and mesenchymal subtype
sec.p: Given the role of GARP in regulating oncogenesis via TGFβ bioavailability, we first sought to determine the role of GARP in several aspects of GBM’s clinical behavior. Therein, we analyzed publicly available transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Chinese Glioma Cancer Atlas (CGGA)59,60 to determine the effects of GARP expression on overall survival in GBM and examine whether GARP correlated with clinicopathological features. Overall, we found that patients with GBM expressing elevated mRNA levels of GARP (LRRC32) demonstrated worsened prognosis (Figure 1A) in both the CGGA and TCGA cohorts. Furthermore, comparison of LRRC32 expression demonstrated elevated expression of GARP in GBM relative to oligodendroma, astrocytoma with or without anaplastic features (Figure 1B) in both the CGGA and TCGA-GBMLGG cohorts. GARP expression was comparable across male and female patients (Supplementary Figure S1A, left) and did not significantly correlate with age at time of diagnosis (Supplementary Figure S1A, right). Similarly, in the CGGA and IvyGap GBM cohorts, LRRC32 expression was significantly elevated in the mesenchymal subtype relative to classical and proneural counterparts (Figure 1C). Additionally, tumors with elevated LRRC32 mRNA expression demonstrated upregulation of mesenchymal subtype-associated transcripts including TGM2, S100A4, and STAT361,62 (Figure 1D).

sec.p: To further substantiate the relationship between GARP and mesenchymal subtype, we analyzed expression of a previously defined GARP-associated mRNA signature (Supplementary Figure S1B) and compared enrichment scores across GBM subtypes. The mesenchymal subtype presented significantly higher GARP-associated signature expression compared to the non-mesenchymal groups (Supplementary Figure S1C, D) which correlated to reduced survival (Supplementary Figure S1E-G). Additionally, we found that the mesenchymal group presented significantly higher GARP-associated signature expression compared to non-mesenchymal groups (Figure 1E).

Consistent with a central role for GARP in promoting TGFβ maturation, GBM patients with elevated LRRC32 expression demonstrated increased TGFβ1, TGFβ2 TGFβ3, and LTBP1 mRNA expression (Figure 1F); furthermore, at the protein level, LRRC32 mRNA-high patients demonstrated greater protein abundance for TGFβI, expression of which is induced upon exposure to TGFβ (Figure 1G). Concordantly, differential expression analysis from TCGA-GBM cohort patients stratified by LRRC32 expression (Figure 1H) identified enrichment in transcripts associated with TGFβ receptor signaling (Figure 1I). Additionally, mesenchymal tumors exhibited enrichment in angiogenesis, myeloid compartment expansion, and T cell exhaustion signatures (Supplementary Figure S1H).

Further gene set enrichment and spatial expression correlation analysis across anatomical features (via the IVY-GAP database) identified increased expression of angiogenesis-associated transcripts (Supplementary Figure S1I) and correlation of LRRC32 expression with regions of hyperplastic blood vessels and microvascular proliferation (Supplementary Figure S1J). These findings align with the known role for TGFβ in promoting angiogenesis, supporting a relationship between GARP expression and tumor-associated vasculature development. Collectively, these results indicate that high GARP expression corresponds to poor outcomes in GBM and delineate GARP as a potential target for intercepting GBM-associated TGFβ signaling and angiogenesis.

sec.title: Impact of GARP expression in GBM on immune cell composition in the TME
sec.p: To elucidate the role of GARP in the GBM TME, we utilized multispectral immunofluorescence to evaluate human GBM specimens obtained from The Ohio State University’s Department of Pathology (Supplementary Table S1). Specimens from ten unique patients were stained for GARP and immune cell markers (CD4, CD8, FOXP3, CD11b). GBM samples exhibited elevated GARP protein expression relative to normal brain (Figure 2A). Tumors exhibited heterogeneous GARP expression (Supplementary Figure S2A), which we designated as “low-GARP” (Figure 2B, left; < 250 GARP+ cells/mm2) and “high-GARP” (Figure 2B, right; > 250 GARP+ cells/mm2) with high-GARP comprising 10-12% of the total scanned tumor area (Figure 2C). There was no significant difference in the mean cell density of tumors between the two classifications (Supplementary Figure S2B). High-GARP regions exhibited increased CD11b+ myeloid cells (Figure 2D) and decreased CD8+ and CD4+ non-Tregs (CD4+/FOXP3-) T cells compared to low-GARP regions (Figure 2E, F). Consistent with these findings, gene set enrichment analysis of LRRC32Low versus LRRC32Hi GBM indicated reduced expression of the PANTHER: T Cell Activation and GO: Adaptive Immune Response (Figure 2G) signatures.

Analysis across patient tissues, mouse glioma models, and TCGA datasets demonstrates that high GARP expression corresponds to an immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment.

sec.p: Myeloid cells are known to induce HGG progression, in part due to TGFβ signaling.63–67 To examine the potential role of GARP in promoting the malignant transformation of glioma, we obtained paired samples from 8 unique patients with LGG that progressed to HGG (Supplementary Table S2) and four commercial tissue microarrays. All glioma samples exhibited regions of elevated GARP staining designated by spatial segmentation algorithm analysis. However, there was a non-significant difference in the average proportion of “high-GARP” tissue area in the HGG vs LGG samples (Supplementary Figure S2C). Consistent with a detrimental role for myeloid cells, HGG samples exhibited increased proportions of myeloid infiltration (Supplementary Figure S2D), including CD206 and iNOS expressing subsets. Nearest neighbor analysis of GARP-low and GARP-high regions determined that immune cells of the same type clustered nearer to each other than to other cell types (Supplementary Figure S2E-G). Homotypic activation-associated clustering has been previously reported to occur during T cell stimulation and the development of antitumor immunity. Consistent with restricted T cell activation, CD8 T cells exhibited greater spatial separation in GARP-high regions (Supplementary Figure S2E-G).

To corroborate the relationship between GARP and suppressive myeloid accumulation, we compared immune infiltrates from intracranially inoculated empty vector control or GARP over expressing CT2A tumors (GARP-OE, Supplementary Figure S2H). GARP-OE CT2A exhibited increased intratumoral macrophages (Figure 2I, left) but not dendritic (Figure 2I, right) or myeloid-derived suppressor cells (Supplementary Figure S2I). Furthermore, GARP-OE tumor-associated macrophages exhibited a tendency to express higher levels of immunoregulatory arginase I (Figure 2J). Additionally, transcriptomic-based immune deconvolution analysis demonstrated increased levels of macrophages and monocytes in GARP-high GBM patients (Figure 2K). Collectively, these results suggest GARP contributes to the development of a macrophage-enriched intratumoral milieu.

sec.title: GARP upregulation predicts GBM stem cell enrichment
sec.p: Accumulation of suppressive myeloid cells has been linked to stem cell-like features in GBM. Furthermore, glioma stem cells (GSCs) are a major therapeutic challenge and niche for glioma recurrence.25,28,68–70 Therein, we next investigated the relationship between GARP and GBM GSC features. LRRC32 mRNA has been difficult to detect by scRNAseq due to low mRNA stability and detection. Indeed, utilizing the TISCH2 single cell database,68,71 we observed very low expression of LRRC32 compared with other GSC markers (e.g. SOX2, CD44, and CD133) (Supplementary Figure S3A). However, based on a public ATAC-seq dataset,69,72 we found that the LRRC32 promotor region was open in human, treatment-naïve GSCs, suggesting that LRRC32 was expressed by GSCs (Supplementary Figure S3B).

Furthermore, gene set enrichment analysis of LRRC32-high GBM detected enhanced expression of the Human Cell Type: Fetal Mesenchymal Progenitor signature (Figure 3A). Additionally, patients from the CCGA GBM cohort with elevated LRRC32 expression demonstrated increased GSC transcript expression (Figure 3B). To validate these findings, we utilized multiplex immunofluorescent analysis via GARP, CD133, CD44, SOX2, and CD31 (Supplementary Table S2) staining of paired LGG/HGG patient samples and examined GARP expression in oligodendrocyte-progenitor-like (OPC)-like GSCs (CD133+/SOX2+), mesenchymal-like GSCs (CD44+/SOX2+), and neoangiogenic vessels (CD31+/CD133+/SOX2-).65 A significant portion of OPC-like and mesenchymal-like GSCs (Figure 3C) and neoangiogenic vessels expressed GARP (Figure 3D, E), suggesting GARP is expressed by tumor cells, two major types of GSCs, and neoangiogenic vessels, all of which are vital to GBM oncogenesis and recurrence.

sec.title: Anti-GARP CAR-T cells exert antitumor efficacy against human GBM models
sec.p: Given the above findings, we believe that GARP can serve as a therapeutic target for GBM. Our group previously generated a humanized, affinity-matured monoclonal antibody (PIIO-1) targeting human GARP (hGARP), which we tested in multiple mouse models of cancer.56 PIIO-1 diminished TGFβ signaling in the TME, reduced metastasis in models of triple-negative breast cancer, exhibited single-agent activity, and improved therapeutic efficacy of anti-PD-1 against multiple cancer types in vivo.38,47 Consistent with PIIO-1’s capacity to intercept GARP-TGFβ binding, predictive structure-based modeling identified the site of latent TGFβ1 and TGFβ3—GARP interaction as the primary binding site of PIIO-1 (Supplementary Figure S4B).

To generate an anti-GARP CAR (Figure 4A, left), we cloned the scFv of PIIO-1 into a CAR construct comprised of a CD8α hinge and transmembrane domain and human 4-1BB and CD3ζ intracellular domains. This anti-GARP CAR construct was cloned into a retroviral vector and expressed in transduced human T cells (Figure 4A, right). Furthermore, we created human GARP (hGARP)-overexpressing (OE) glioma cell lines derived from luciferase expressing parental cells (U87-WT and U87-hGARP-OE [human]; C57BL/6 syngeneic GBM line CT2A-WT and CT2A-hGARP-OE [C57BL/6]; GL261-WT and GL261-hGARP-OE [C57BL/6]) (Supplementary Figures S4C, S2H).

In vitro assays demonstrate dose-dependent cytotoxicity and cytokine production by anti-GARP CAR-T cells against GARP-expressing glioma lines and patient-derived xenografts. In vivo studies in mouse glioblastoma models show tumor reduction by bioluminescence imaging, improved survival with anti-GARP CAR-T treatment compared to controls, and histological evidence of reduced tumor burden. sec.p: Next, we examined the anti-tumor activity of anti-GARP CAR-T against human glioma U87. We found that anti-GARP CAR-T cells induced tumor cell lysis (Figure 4B), and secretion of IFNγ, TNFα, and IL-2 (Figure 4C) in vitro. Anti-GARP CAR T cells exhibited increased proportions of effector memory-like cells alongside reductions in exhausted, regulatory CD4 + and central memory-like cells (Figure 4D).

To evaluate anti-tumor efficacy of human anti-GARP CAR-T in vivo, we used an orthotopic xenograft model of GBM in NOD-SCID-gamma (NSG) mice (Figure 4E). After confirming tumor engraftment, mice with stereotactically implanted U87-hGARP-OE tumors were randomized and treated with intratumoral infusion of EV-T or anti-GARP CAR-T cells (1 × 105 cells/mouse). IVIS imaging demonstrated decreased tumor burden and prolonged survival in mice treated with anti-GARP CAR-T relative to control (Figure 4F, P < .0001, log-rank test). Endpoint H&E and GARP staining demonstrated EV T-treated mice had significantly greater tumor burden and GARP expression; anti-GARP CAR-T-treated mice showed no evidence of residual disease or aberrant GARP expression (Figure 4G). Similarly, GARP expression remained detectable but reduced on tumor cells after coculture with GARP-targeting CAR-T cells (Supplementary Figure S4D).

To validate these findings in the context of endogenous GARP expression, we utilized DK-MG human GBM and patient-derived GBM xenograft (h-GBM-PDX) cells. Both DK-MG and h-GBM-PDX cells demonstrated low, but detectable levels of GARP (Figure 4H). GARP-targeting CAR-T induced killing of DK-MG and h-GBM-PDX in vitro although cytotoxicity against PDX242 was lower than that observed for PDX46 and DK-MG (Figure 4I, J). Furthermore, anti-GARP CAR-T treatment of NSG implanted intracranially with DK-MG exhibited efficient tumor growth control compared to PBS or non-targeting control CAR-T treatment (Supplementary Figure S4E, F). These data affirm that human-derived anti-GARP CAR-T cells effectively eliminate orthotopic tumors in murine GBM models.

sec.title: In vitro and in vivo activity of anti-GARP CAR-T cells against murine syngeneic GBM tumors in LRRC32 knockin mice
sec.p: Next, we examined the anti-tumor activity of murine anti-GARP CAR-T against murine glioma in the immunocompetent host.73 Splenic C57BL/6 T cells were activated with anti-CD3/CD28 followed by retroviral anti-GARP CAR transduction. After confirming GARP expression (Figure 5A), we co-cultured CT-2A and GL-261 (wild type and hGARP overexpressing) with anti-GARP CAR-T; like human anti-GARP CAR-T, murine CAR-T elicited GARP-dependent cytotoxicity against hGARP-expressing murine GBM cells (Figure 5B), with concurrent cytokine secretion (Figure 5C).

In immune-competent human GARP knock-in mice, bioluminescence imaging shows tumor regression, survival is significantly prolonged in CAR-T–treated mice compared to controls, and blood counts remain stable, indicating no major hematologic toxicity.

sec.p: To further determine the efficacy and safety of anti-GARP CAR-T, hLRRC32KI mice (Figure 5D)74,75 with stereotactically implanted CT2A hGARP-OE tumors underwent lymphodepleting irradiation (5Gy) and randomization into EV-T or CAR-T treatment groups. Anti-GARP CAR-T treatment reduced tumor growth with several mice exhibiting tumor regression (Figure 5E, F, Supplementary Figure S5A), while mice in the control group demonstrated tumor progression. Overall, mice receiving anti-GARP CAR-T showed reduced tumor burden (Figure 5E; P = .0007, mixed effects analysis) and prolonged survival versus controls (median OS 51 versus 35 days) (Figure 5F; P < .0001, log-rank test).

To monitor tolerability, we collected weekly blood draws. Despite an initial drop in WBC and platelets after irradiation, anti-GARP CAR-T treated mice did not suffer from more thrombocytopenia or other hematological toxicities versus control (Figure 5G, H). These data suggest that intracranial anti-GARP CAR-T targets tumor cells and prolongs survival, while not eliciting hematological toxicity or overt immune-related adverse events.

sec.title: Anti-GARP CAR-T cells did not elicit overt toxicity when administered systemically.
sec.p: Next, we evaluated the potential for on-target/off-tumor toxicity via intravenous infusion. We administered 1 × 106 murine anti-GARP CAR-T or control CAR-T (against EGFRvIII) via tail vein injection into non-tumor-bearing, irradiation lymphodepleted hLRRC32KI mice and monitored body weight, mortality, and serum cytokines for 60 days. No mortality or significant changes in body weight were observed (Figure 6A). Platelet counts and serum cytokine levels were stable in both groups (Figure 6B–D).

Body weight, platelet counts, and serum cytokines remain stable compared to controls. Immunofluorescence staining of human tissue microarrays shows low-intensity GARP expression in immune tissues, vascular linings, and basement membranes. sec.p: Furthermore, we performed immunofluorescence staining to evaluate expression in normal human tissue microarrays and detected GARP staining in a small number of tissues (vessels, esophagus, cervix, kidney, tonsil, and thymus) (Figure 6E). Staining in immune tissue and vasculature is expected, given the function of GARP. Staining in the cervix and kidney was low-intensity and limited to vessels/basement membrane compared to high-intensity GARP staining in GBM. Consistent with these findings, transcriptomic analysis of normal human tissues indicated low LRRC32 expression across all vital tissues (Figure 6F).

To better profile potential off-target interactions between our GARP-targeting construct, we utilized a Retrogenix cell microarray assay, which interrogates the interaction of antibodies/Fab fragments with a library of 6,500 full-length human plasma membrane and tethered secreted proteins. Screening of the GARP-targeting PIIO-1 antibody (20 μg/ml) identified only three specific significant interactions (Median SNR ≥ 1), one of which was GARP. The other two targets were the high-affinity Fc receptors FCGR1A and FCGR2A, consistent with the presence of an intact Fc domain within PIIO-1 (Figure 6G). Collectively, these data further underscore the safety and the translatability of our anti-GARP CAR-T therapeutically.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Adoptive T cell transfer therapy with CAR-T, endogenous T cells, or other engineered T cells continues to expand in scale and indication, with solid tumor targets gaining traction with each new iteration. GBM is an attractive candidate for CAR-T therapy due to the limited efficacy of standard of care treatments and immune checkpoint blockers.24 In this study, we demonstrate that elevated GARP expression in human GBM correlates with poor overall survival, mesenchymal subtype, and gene signatures associated with angiogenesis and immune exclusion in the tumor microenvironment. We are also the first to report the generation and preclinical efficacy of anti-GARP CAR-T against multiple models of GBM, including patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models without significant toxicity. Our data suggest that GARP is a prime target antigen for CAR-T therapy of GBM due to (1) its restricted expression in GBM versus normal brain; (2) its contribution to the development of an immunosuppressive TME via activating latent TGFβ40; and (3) its expression by GBM stem cells and tumor-associated vasculature. Thus, anti-GARP CAR-T approach simultaneously targets multiple pro-GBM axes.

A major concern with targeting GARP via CAR-T is the potential for on-target, off-tumor toxicity. However, we did not observe unexpected side effects of anti-GARP CAR-T in our preclinical human GARP knock-in mouse models. The fear that our anti-GARP CAR-T cells could cause platelet destruction was unfounded for 3 key reasons: (a) our anti-GARP antibody PIIO-1 is highly specific without off-target binding activities; (b) platelets are major producers of latent TGFβ.34 As a result, all de novo synthesized GARP molecules in megakaryocytes and platelets are pre-complexed with LTGFβ; (c) our anti-GARP CAR-T construct recognize the LTGFβ-binding site of GARP and only bind to LTGFβ-free GARP.76 Thus, biochemically, our anti-GARP constructs spare megakaryocytes and platelets. Indeed, no thrombocytopenia was observed when GARP CAR-T cells were given to either tumor-free or GBM-bearing human GARP knockin mice. Together, our data suggests that using anti-GARP CAR-T cells will be potentially safe in human patients.

Our extensive datamining and TME analyses suggest that GARP is not merely a biomarker for GBM. However, a fundamental question we did not address in this study was the underlying mechanism and biology of GARP-LTGFβ axis in the oncogenesis of GBM. One possibility is that GARP plays both cancer-intrinsic and extrinsic roles in the development and treatment resistance of GBM. It may also be involved in the progression of glioma from low grade to high grade, a hypothesis we plan to address using our genetic models67 in the future. The study of multi-faceted roles of GARP in GBM could also lead to a better understanding of how adaptive immunity is initiated or constrained in the brain. In this regard, the GARP biology in regulatory T cells40,77,78 and brain vasculature will be especially noteworthy and important to study and understand, for potentially broadening our anti-GARP CAR-T therapy beyond primary CNS tumors in the future. Additionally, further study is needed to compare the relative efficacy of CAR constructs utilizing 41BB versus CD28 intracellular signaling domains.

Collectively, we have developed a unique, effective, and tolerable anti-GARP CAR-T for GBM in preclinical models. The clinical utility of our anti-GARP CAR-T platform is being evaluated by our first-in-human phase I clinical trial for patients with recurrent GBM (NCT06964737).
